why: One table, read by both halves of the app, so the two answers to "can this
laptop dial that?" cannot drift apart in silence.
Rust's `cloudbox::is_dialable` is the authority: every place that reaches a
machine passes through it, whether the address came out of the machine book
or out of the connect wizard's form. The frontend keeps one small copy
(`lib/place/boot.ts`) because a form validates as you type and a button that
opens a terminal has to be enabled or disabled before anything is asked —
neither can afford a round trip per keystroke.
A copy that quietly stopped agreeing would show up as a button that is
enabled and then fails, or worse, one that is disabled on an address that
works. So both read this file. Change one implementation and its own test
fails here; change the rule for real and both have to be updated together.
Note what is NOT a rule: a space, a quote or an apostrophe in the KEY PATH.
That path never reaches a shell unquoted — see quoting.cases.json — so
refusing it would only lock people out of their own key.

cases.why: an address and a key: the ordinary machine
a name rather than a number, and a key under the home directory
dashes and digits are what real hostnames are made of
a space in the key path is quoted, not refused
a host that is really an ssh option: the whole reason this check exists
a second command hiding in a host
a substitution hiding in a host
a space would split one argument into two
the same, on the login side
no login is not a login
a key path of spaces means the box will ask for a password nobody can type
255 characters is the longest a host may be
